title: Detection Strategy for Wi-Fi Networks
summary: This detection strategy covers wireless network activity that supports adversary use of Wi-Fi for access and collection, matching technique T1669 across enterprise wireless estates. It matters because the wireless layer is the one part of the estate an attacker can reach from a parked car, and its events rarely appear in the same platform as endpoint telemetry. The data that makes it possible is controller and wireless intrusion detection alerts, authentication server records for network access, and sensor reports about access points that were not deployed by the organisation. It fails in practice because office buildings contain dense legitimate overlap from neighbouring businesses and personal hotspots, so rules that alert on every new service set identifier, or SSID, drown the team and stop being reviewed.

beginner.definition: This detection watches the wireless network around your buildings. It looks for signs that someone is running a fake access point or forcing devices off the real one. A wireless access point is the box that devices connect to for Wi-Fi.
beginner.whyItMatters: Wireless signals pass through walls and reach the street. An attacker does not need a badge to be near your network. A fake access point can collect passwords or send users to a lookalike page. Devices that are forced offline may reconnect to the attacker instead of to your network.
howItWorks: Wireless sensors and controllers listen to every radio frame in the area and record what they hear.
The sensors report new network names, sudden disconnection frames, and access points with no known owner.
The controller forwards those reports to the central log platform, called a security information and event management system, or SIEM.
The rule keeps only events from locations where your own wireless team has approved and installed equipment.
It compares the reported device address with the approved inventory of access points.
Events that do not match the inventory become an alert with the sensor location.
beginner.example: Imagine a night watchman who walks the same route every hour. He knows every door and every lamp. One night he sees a new sign on a door that nobody fitted. He does not open it, he calls the manager. A wireless sensor reports an access point that nobody fitted in the same way.
takeaways: Wireless coverage leaves the building, so treat the air around your site as an attack surface.
A sudden flood of disconnection frames can be a sign that someone is pushing devices off your network.
Compare every reported access point with your own hardware inventory.

objectives: Describe the wireless events that indicate rogue access points, evil twin access points and forced disconnection of clients
Identify the controller, sensor and authentication server records that capture wireless activity
Correlate a reported access point with the approved hardware inventory and its physical location
Write a detection rule that alerts on wireless anomalies and scope it to the sites you can physically investigate
Explain the limits of wireless detection and what it cannot prove on its own
dataSources: Wireless controller and wireless intrusion detection sensor events for rogue access point and evil twin detection
Wireless authentication and association logs from the network access control server showing repeated failed joins
Wireless sensor reports of management frame activity such as deauthentication and disassociation floods
Site survey and approved wireless access point inventory with physical sensor locations
logic: The pattern is a wireless event that contradicts your own known infrastructure: an access point that broadcasts an approved network name but does not appear in the hardware inventory, a burst of deauthentication frames aimed at many clients from a single source radio, or a flood of authentication failures at one sensor location. The fields that must be correlated are the broadcasting device address, the network name, the sensor identifier and its site, the channel, and the time window. The benign case is a neighbouring business, a visitor hotspot, or an administrator testing a new access point that is already recorded in the change calendar; the malicious case shows an unapproved device imitating an approved network name near a sensor that covers staff areas.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Wireless anomaly - unapproved access point or forced disconnection
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: wireless
# detection:
#   selection_rogue:
#     event_type: rogue access point detected
#     ssid_match: true
#   selection_flood:
#     event_type: deauthentication flood
#   condition: selection_rogue or selection_flood
# level: medium
falsePositives: Neighbouring businesses whose access points broadcast a similar but not identical network name inside shared office buildings
Personal mobile hotspots carried by staff and visitors that appear as unapproved access points during working hours
Network engineers staging new access points on the production network before the inventory record is updated
Wireless testing tools used during a scheduled site survey that deliberately send management frames
tuningNotes: Scope the rule to sensors inside your own buildings and drop detections whose signal strength indicates a device outside the perimeter, because those are usually neighbours and cannot be investigated. Baseline the network names your organisation uses and require an exact or near exact name match rather than alerting on every new name. Reduce the deauthentication alert to bursts above a threshold per minute so that normal roaming and a single client retry do not fire it. Narrowing this way means you lose awareness of an attacker who uses a different network name to lure users, so keep a separate lower severity report for all new network names seen near reception and meeting rooms.
